title: Real-world right triangles
summary: A ladder against a wall makes a right-angled triangle — spot it, then use Pythagoras to find its length.
alt: A ladder of length {{L|2}} m leaning against a vertical wall: its top is {{h|1}} m high and its foot is {{d|1}} m from the wall.

hyp.label: Hypotenuse
hyp.text: The side opposite the right angle. It is always the longest side.

legA.label: Shorter side 1
legA.text: One of the two sides that meet at the right angle.

legB.label: Shorter side 2
legB.text: The other side that meets at the right angle.

steps.title: The situation
steps.narration: A construction worker is on a ladder placed against a **vertical wall**. The top of the ladder is **{{h|1}} m** above the ground and the foot of the ladder is **{{d|1}} m** from the wall. How **long** is the ladder?

steps.title: Spot the right triangle
steps.narration: A wall stands **straight up** from flat ground, so they meet at a **right angle**. That gives a **right-angled triangle**: the wall, the ground and the ladder. The ladder faces the right angle, so the ladder is the [[hyp|hypotenuse]]. Call its length **x**.

steps.title: Write the theorem
steps.narration: Let the length of the ladder be **x m**. Using Pythagoras' Theorem, \[ \role{hyp}{x^2} = \role{legB}{ {{h|1}}^2 } + \role{legA}{ {{d|1}}^2 } \]

steps.title: Calculate
steps.narration: Square each side and add: \[\begin{aligned} x^2 &= {{h^2|2}} + {{d^2|2}} \\ &= {{h^2+d^2|2}} \end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Take the square root
steps.narration: \[ x = \sqrt{ {{h^2+d^2|2}} } = \role{ans}{ {{L|2}} } \]The ladder is about **{{L|2}} m** long (3 s.f.). It is longer than the height ({{h|1}} m) — a sensible answer.

steps.title: The same idea everywhere
steps.narration: Ladders, poles, cables, distances on a map: **sketch a rough diagram**, mark the **right angle**, label the unknown as **x**, then use Pythagoras' Theorem. Drag the sliders to change the ladder, then try the challenges.

formulas.title: The ladder
formulas.text: The wall, the ground and the ladder form a right-angled triangle; the ladder is the hypotenuse.

challenges.title: Find the ladder
challenges.prompt: A ladder reaches **2 m** up a wall and its foot is **1.5 m** from the wall. How long is the ladder?
challenges.hint: The ladder is the hypotenuse: x² = 2² + 1.5².

challenges.title: How high does it reach?
challenges.prompt: A **2.5 m** ladder has its foot **0.7 m** from a wall. How high up the wall does it reach?
challenges.hint: Now the ladder is the hypotenuse and the height is a shorter side — subtract: 2.5² − 0.7².

challenges.title: Which side is the hypotenuse?
challenges.prompt: In the ladder triangle, which side is the **hypotenuse**?
challenges.hint: It faces the right angle between the wall and the ground.
challenges.explain: The wall and the ground meet at the right angle, so the ladder — opposite it — is the hypotenuse.

intro: Pythagoras' Theorem helps with ladders, poles, cables and distances. The skill is **spotting the right-angled triangle** hidden in the picture.
takeaways: Look for the **right angle** — a wall and the ground, two roads at a crossing, north and east.
**Sketch** a rough diagram and label every length, using **x** for the unknown.
The side opposite the right angle (the ladder, the cable, the straight-line distance) is the **hypotenuse**.
Check your answer is sensible: the hypotenuse must be the **longest** side.

notes.title: Journey problems
notes.text: For "walks 5 km north then 12 km east" draw the two legs at 90° — the straight-line distance back to the start is the hypotenuse.

challengeIntro: Try a few ladders of your own.
